title: Baroque Drama
objective: After this level you can explain how Baroque art used movement and emotion to grab the viewer.
summary: Baroque, named after a misshapen pearl, began in Italy around 1600. The Church wanted art that stirred faith, so artists used diagonals, motion and illusion, like Rubens's cross and Pozzo's fake dome.

cards.headline: Baroque started out as an insult. It probably means a lumpy pearl.
cards.body: The word likely comes from barroco, Portuguese for an irregularly shaped pearl, and for centuries critics used it to mean odd and overdone. The art it names began in Italy in the late 1500s and filled the 1600s. It aimed for drama, movement and emotion. It wanted to grab you.

cards.headline: The Church wanted art that moved you
cards.body: After the Council of Trent (1545 to 1563), the Catholic Church gave art a job: strengthen ordinary people's faith. The pictures had to be clear and lifelike, so anyone could read them without a scholar standing by. And they had to use dramatic effects that stirred real feeling. A calm, clever puzzle for experts would not do. The Church wanted art that hit you in the chest.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: Baroque drama had a job, to stir the faith of ordinary people.

cards.fact: Rubens caught the cross halfway up.
cards.context: In The Elevation of the Cross (about 1610), painted for Antwerp's cathedral, muscular men strain to heave the cross upright. It cuts across the picture on a steep diagonal, stuck between lying down and standing. You arrive mid-heave, while the effort is still going on. Stormy diagonals and full-blooded bodies like these are seen as the essence of Baroque painting.

cards.headline: A dome that isn't there
cards.body: Walk into the church of Sant'Ignazio in Rome and look up: a dome rises over you. It's paint. In 1685 Andrea Pozzo painted it on a flat surface, because the Jesuits had apparently run out of money for a real one. A disc set in the floor marks the one spot where the illusion works. Step off it and the dome gives itself away.

cards.headline: Baroque drama: felt
learned: Baroque began in Italy around 1600, named after a lumpy pearl
The Church wanted art that stirred ordinary people's faith
Rubens used a steep diagonal to catch motion
Pozzo painted a fake dome that works from one floor disc

questions.prompt: What marks the spot where Pozzo's painted dome in Sant'Ignazio looks real?

options.label: A disc set in the church floor
A window cut into the ceiling
options.rationale: The dome is painted on a flat surface, no opening needed.

options.label: A mirror hung beside the altar
options.rationale: The trick is where you stand, marked on the floor.

options.label: A painted arrow on one column
options.rationale: A disc in the floor does the job.

questions.explanation: A disc in the floor marks the one viewpoint where Pozzo's flat painting looks like a real dome.

questions.prompt: Why does Rubens show the cross on a steep diagonal, halfway up?

options.label: To fit a very tall cross on a small panel
Because the Church required crosses to lean
options.rationale: No such rule; the diagonal is Rubens's drama.

options.label: To catch the moment in motion, mid-effort
To copy the calm balance of earlier altarpieces
options.rationale: Calm balance is exactly what the diagonal breaks.

questions.explanation: A cross stuck between lying and standing puts you in the middle of the struggle: movement and drama, the Baroque signature.

questions.prompt: Level 1 tied the Baroque of the 1600s to drama, movement and emotion. Why did the Catholic Church want art like that?

options.label: Rich collectors wanted exciting pictures for their homes
options.rationale: Here the patron is the Church, and the goal is faith.

options.label: Dramatic, clear images could stir ordinary people's faith
Painters had run out of calm subjects to paint
options.rationale: The push came from the Church after the Council of Trent.

options.label: Only experts were allowed to look at church art
options.rationale: The opposite: art had to be clear to anyone.

questions.explanation: After the Council of Trent, the Church wanted clear, lifelike, dramatic art to strengthen the public's faith.
